articles.body: Europe Operations NATO boosts Black Sea surveillance amid attacks on shipping Adis Ajdin October 21, 2026 1 335 1 minute read NATO is deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea following a series of deadly attacks on merchant shipping off Romania and Bulgaria. The move follows a meeting of the alliance’s North Atlantic Council in Brussels on Tuesday, with members also sending intelligence personnel and explosives investigation teams to the region. NATO military spokesman colonel Martin O’Donnell said the additional assets would strengthen surveillance and reconnaissance, with the emphasis on improving intelligence sharing and identifying threats to shipping. Bulgaria has already confirmed that a US Navy P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft has begun reconnaissance flights over the Black Sea following its request for assistance from NATO. Bulgarian prime minister Rumen Radev said allies had responded quickly to Sofia’s appeal, with further support expected. Four merchant ships have been attacked in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone over the past month, two of which sank. Allied specialists are also expected to help investigate the October 13 drone attack on the Malta-flagged general cargoship Chelsea 3 off Bulgaria. All 15 crewmembers were rescued, and investigators are examining recovered drone debris to establish the type of weapon used. The latest NATO response comes after a string of attacks on commercial vessels, including two chemical tankers off Romania last week. One of them, the Comoros-flagged Yara J , caught fire after a suspected drone strike inside Romanian territorial waters near the Sulina Canal. The crew managed to extinguish the blaze without outside assistance. The attacks have increasingly threatened shipping routes serving Ukraine’s Danube and Black Sea ports, adding to pressure on grain exports and pushing war-risk insurance costs higher. Russia’s defence ministry separately claimed on Tuesday that its forces had struck three cargo vessels at the Ukrainian port of Reni and another two heading towards Odesa, alleging that the ships were being used for military purposes. NATO has not formally attributed the recent attacks off Romania and Bulgaria to Russia, which has denied responsibility for those incidents. Despite the worsening security situation, Bulgarian authorities said commercial shipping to the Black Sea ports of Varna and Burgas was continuing, with no decline in vessel traffic reported. articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: Red Sea container traffic set for full return in Q1
articles.summary: Trends in international ocean logistics seem even more confusing than usual lately: more Iranian attacks but more Hormuz traffic; more crude exports but oil prices still around $100 per barrel; more risk of Houthi attacks on passing ships, but more container vessels returning to the Red Sea anyway. Iran has stepped...
articles.body: Trends in international ocean logistics seem even more confusing than usual lately: more Iranian attacks but more Hormuz traffic; more crude exports but oil prices still around $100 per barrel; more risk of Houthi attacks on passing ships, but more container vessels returning to the Red Sea anyway. Iran has stepped up the frequency of attacks on vessels around the Strait of Hormuz, partially because transits and crude flows through the waterway have increased in recent weeks. Last week an Iranian projectile sunk a Dubai-linked container vessel, indicating that even some container ships are taking the risk of transiting the strait, though most traffic still comprises tankers. Despite some estimates that the increase in tankers exiting the Persian Gulf is contributing to Middle East crude exports approaching pre-war levels, crude prices – still pricing in elevated risk – remain high. Houthi-Saudi violence is intensifying, with recent Houthi advances along the Red Sea increasing its potential leverage over maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the likelihood of attacks on passing vessels. Despite that heightened risk – which since late 2023 had been enough to divert the vast majority of container traffic away from the Red Sea – container carriers continue their steady march back through the Suez, with estimates that transits will fully recover during Q1 of the coming year. Why carriers are more comfortable going back now than during similar, earlier high-risk stretches is a good question. The answer is probably a mix of high current fuel costs and congestion levels with evolving geopolitical considerations. These considerations may include, as Peter Tirschwell recently pointed out, Houthi interest in security and stability for most Red Sea traffic that could somewhat legitimize the group in relation to the West – alongside increased pressure directed at Saudi Arabia and its passing vessels. Whatever the reasons, that the Red Sea container rebound is happening gradually instead of all at once should mitigate the extent of schedule disruptions and vessel bunching that will occur as more vessels arrive earlier than slotted. That this restoration unfolded post the early-July Asia – Europe demand peak, and will continue through the coming low demand months will also mean less disruption to shippers than if the return coincided with peak season. Current port congestion levels – though backlogs and delays are finally easing at Far East hubs – continues to absorb some container capacity, and will help carriers maintain rate levels even as effective capacity increases from vessels circulating more quickly via the Red Sea. Overall though, the Red Sea return – if geopolitics allow its completion – increases the overcapacity risk for carriers in 2027. At the moment, even with Red Sea-driven effective capacity increases and slumping demand on Asia – Europe trades, spot rates are recently trending up on these lanes after months of declines. Asia – N. Europe Freightos Baltic Index rates climbed 6% last week to $3,442/FEU and prices to the Mediterranean increased 3% to $3,927/FEU on recent GRIs aimed at putting pressure on rates as 2027 long term contract negotiations get underway. Some forwarders are skeptical however, that increases will stick given current market conditions. Transpacific ocean rates were stable but still highly elevated last week at $8,126/FEU to the West Coast, with prices up 1% to $9,700/FEU for the East Coast. Daily rates so far this week are showing signs of increase – despite expectations that volumes are finally cooling – possibly due to capacity reductions as the lanes enter slow season. Last month some carriers announced plans for significanttransatlantic container price increases in October. So far though transatlantic spot rates have increased only about $200/FEU to $2,850/FEU since the end of September. Prices are however 25% higher than a year ago, possibly reflecting upward pressure from elevated bunker costs. In air cargo, the EU is set to introduce a November 1st €2 small parcel handling fee on top of the €3 customs surcharge introduced in July for low value imports that previously entered via the de minimis exemption. This additional fee could increase the China – Europe e-commerce volume draw down seen since July, which has led to some downward pressure on air cargo rates and shifted freighter capacity to other lanes. Freightos Air Index data show ex-China rates increased last week, possibly on a post-Golden Week backlog rebound or signalling the start of peak season pressure. Prices posted a sharp 19% gain to $6.88/kg to the US and an 8% climb to $3.87/kg to Europe. But while the global benchmark is 30% higher than a year ago on elevated fuel costs and volume growth – with transpacific rates 25% higher year on year – Asia – Europe prices are down 3% compared to last October, possibly reflecting e-commerce volume adjustments on this lane. articles.body: Containers Middle East Iraqi Line returns to Gulf container trade after 50 years Sam Chambers October 21, 2026 0 1,651 1 minute read ICTSI ICTSI Iraq’s national shipping line is returning to scheduled container services in the Gulf after more than half a century, as the country seeks to rebuild maritime connections disrupted by the Strait of Hormuz crisis. According to Alphaliner, Iraqi Maritime Line is deploying the 902 teu Basrah on an eight-day shuttle linking Jebel Ali in Dubai with Umm Qasr, Iraq’s principal container gateway. The first sailing was scheduled to depart Jebel Ali yesterday, arriving in Umm Qasr two days later. Iraq’s transport ministry has described the initiative as the national carrier’s first regular Gulf operation since the mid-1960s. The relaunch comes as Iraqi container supply chains have been radically reshaped since the Hormuz shipping crisis erupted at the end of February. Growing volumes have been diverted to Jordan’s Red Sea port of Aqaba before travelling overland into Iraq through the Trebil border crossing. According to the Jordan Shipping Association, Aqaba handled 37,182 Iraq-bound transit containers during the first seven months of 2026, compared with just 3,599 during the corresponding period last year, a 933% increase. Maersk has introduced landbridge services connecting Aqaba with Iraq, while CMA CGM has offered alternative routings through Aqaba for southern Iraq and Turkey’s Mersin for northern destinations. The French carrier has also established multimodal connections through Saudi Arabia’s Jeddah and ports in Oman and the UAE. Other carriers have maintained limited maritime connections through smaller feeder vessels. Hapag-Lloyd outlined a routing in July whereby containers are discharged at Khorfakkan, outside the Strait of Hormuz, before being trucked across the UAE to Sharjah or Jebel Ali and transferred onto third-party feeder vessels serving Iraq and other upper Gulf destinations. The new Iraqi service will provide a dedicated national shipping connection with the region’s largest container hub, although vessels operating between Jebel Ali and Umm Qasr must still navigate the increasingly dangerous Strait of Hormuz. articles.title: North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms
articles.summary: The UK regulator has given Shell-backed Adura the go-ahead for a North Sea gas field following a courtroom showdown with environmental campaigners.
articles.body: Authorities & Government October 21, 2026 · 9 hours ago North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms The UK regulator has given Shell-backed Adura the go-ahead for a North Sea gas field following a courtroom showdown with environmental campaigners. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Jackdaw platform Source: Aker Solutions One of the North Sea’s most controversial gas projects has clawed its way back from the courtroom after climate legal challenges threw its future into limbo. Adura, an incorporated joint venture between UK-headquartered Shell and Norway’s Equinor, has now secured clearance to push ahead with Jackdaw, a high-stakes field designed to heat millions of British homes, even as environmental battles look set to rage on. The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) has granted development and production consent for the Jackdaw field off the coast of northeast Scotland to Adura, following the SoS’ consideration of the company’s environmental statement and agreement to the grant of consent. Stuart Payn , NSTA’s Chief Executive, commented: “After robust scrutiny we have today granted consent for the Jackdaw field development which allows the owners to proceed with their project and produce gas from the field upon completion of development work. “This project will support the UK’s energy security by providing domestically produced gas, generate tax revenues, safeguard supply chain jobs, use existing infrastructure, and have an emissions intensity well below the UK average.” Jackdaw has the potential to deliver around 6% of projected UK North Sea gas production, which is considered to be enough fuel to heat the equivalent of 1.4 million homes at a time when older gas fields are reaching the end of their production. Payn added: "Now is the time to move forward at pace and we welcome the government's approval in allowing us permission to consider a small number of new out of round licences ahead of forthcoming legislation." The field, located approximately 250 kilometers east of Aberdeen, is expected to be among the lowest-emission developments on the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS), while supporting jobs and bolstering Britain’s energy security. Previously, the NSTA gave consent on June 1, 2022, to develop the Jackdaw project after the Offshore Petroleum Regulator for Environment & Decommissioning (OPRED) agreed to the grant of consent for the development following an assessment of the environmental impacts of the project. However, Greenpeace asked the Scottish Court to review the grant of consent and OPRED’s agreement to the grant of consent in relation to the planning application and the need to consider not only the emissions from the platform’s operations but also the emissions when the gas is used by customers. The UK Supreme Court issued a judgment in a case referred to as ‘Finch’ in 2024 , regarding a proposed oil well in Surrey that was approved by the local council in 2019, ruling that the approval should also have considered the emissions produced by the oil’s end use as well as those emissions caused by the oil well’s operations. Afterward, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled on January 30, 2025, that the previous government’s decision to approve the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil fields was unlawful. As a result, the court overturned the decision, accepting Uplift’s argument that the government failed to consider the emissions that would be caused by burning the oil and gas produced by these fields when it approved them. Related Articles Fossil Energy Multi-billion projects at stake: Another blow for UK’s largest untapped oil & gas duo but Shell, Equinor, and Ithaca remain upbeat 14 min read Adura has continued to comply with all laws and regulations relating to the Jackdaw project situated in blocks 30/02a, 30/03a, and 30/02d of the United Kingdom Continental Shelf that lies in a water depth of approximately 78 meters. The field is located in the Central North Sea (CNS), 30 kilometers southeast of the Shearwater platform and adjacent to the UK/Norway median line. Jackdaw is a gas/condensate development comprising a not permanently attended wellhead platform with four wells, tied back to the Shearwater hub via a 31-kilometer pipeline. The steel jacket and topside were installed in August 2023 and October 2025, respectively. The pipeline was laid in July 2024 and the drilling activities were completed in early 2026. While the latest approval marks a major turning point, the environmental battles are not entirely over since environmental groups like Greenpeace remain strongly opposed to the development of the North Sea oil and gas projects, which have become a primary battleground for climate litigation. As a result, activists continue to scrutinize these approvals. By resubmitting the required environmental statements and clearing this regulatory hurdle, the Jackdaw project has overcome the specific legal blockades that previously stalled it, allowing developers to finally move forward even if political and activist friction persists. Responding to the government giving the Jackdaw gas field the go-ahead, Sam Richards , CEO of Britain Remade, said: “Britain is going to need gas for decades to come, as even the Climate Change Committee recognises. The choice is not between gas and no gas, but between gas produced in British waters and gas shipped in from abroad at higher cost and with higher emissions. “But while we should use what we have, the North Sea is a declining basin, and we need to transition to homegrown clean power. Britain’s always-on electricity should come from new clean nuclear, both gigawatt-scale reactors and small modular reactors that can be sited in far more places than their bigger cousins. “Right now Britain is the most expensive place in the world to build new nuclear. Ministers should urgently implement the Fingleton Review in full in order to drive down cost. The government should also commit to a new small modular reactor at Dungeness without delay.” Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel
articles.summary: Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident...
articles.body: Europe Maritime CEO Operations Tech HarborLab: Why shipping’s husbandry bills are still stuck in Excel Splash October 21, 2026 0 392 3 minutes read HarborLab HarborLab Shipping has spent years tightening voyage costs, bunker procurement and commercial port expenses, but one sizeable part of the bill remains comparatively untouched: husbandry. For Antonis Malaxianakis, founder and CEO of Athens-based port cost management platform HarborLab, that blind spot is particularly evident around bunkering, crew changes and stores, where technical departments can still be managing substantial sums through spreadsheets and email. “Husbandry calls have never carried the same profit and loss visibility as commercial port calls,” Malaxianakis tells Maritime CEO. The absence of cargo revenue against which expenditure can be measured has meant these calls have escaped some of the scrutiny applied elsewhere in ship operations. At the same time, the invoices are anything but simple. A port call can generate hundreds of pages involving port authorities, pilots, tug operators, customs brokers, bunker suppliers, repair companies and other parties. Pricing may vary even within the same port, while additional items such as demurrage, detention, congestion surcharges and equipment rental can emerge later. For Malaxianakis, who worked in disbursement departments at Thenamaris and Product Shipping & Trading before founding HarborLab in 2020, the problem is less about a lack of attention from technical managers than the tools available to them. The gap is particularly pronounced in Asia. “One data point from our analysis makes the structural difference concrete: 75% of technical managers in APAC still manage husbandry bills in Excel today, compared with 40% in EMEA,” he says. Across much of Asia, technical managers have direct control over dayto-day port expenditure but often lack a live reference against which an agent’s quote can be checked. HarborLab sees that combination as one reason APAC has become a priority market. “That combination, direct spending authority paired with heavier reliance on manual tools, does leave APAC more exposed to inconsistent pricing,” Malaxianakis explains.“The decision-maker already controls the budget; they’re simply working without the visibility to know whether what’s being paid is fair.” HarborLab argues that the difference between checking whether an invoice matches a quoted tariff and determining whether the quoted price was reasonable in the first place is where much of the potential saving sits. The company points to a controlled three-month trial with one customer in which half of a fleet remained on its existing disbursement account process while the other half moved to HarborLab. The HarborLab-managed vessels generated $220,000 in savings compared with $70,000 on the other half. “The gap isn’t down to one single lever, but the largest multiplier is benchmarking,” Malaxianakis says. “Manual review, however careful, can only check an invoice against a tariff document or a prior year’s DA; it can confirm a charge matches what was quoted, not whether the quote itself was fair.” HarborLab checks individual expense items against its database covering more than 1,400 ports. The system also picks up incorrect and duplicated charges, with the company then taking discrepancies back to agents in an effort to turn the finding into a credit. Benchmarking port calls is not as straightforward as comparing a bunker price or a standard commodity rate, however. Local tariffs, vessel types and individual port requirements mean two apparently similar services can legitimately carry very different costs. Malaxianakis argues that broad averages would therefore create another problem rather than solve the existing one. “Every benchmark is built at the level of port, vessel type, and expense category, not as one blended number, so a crane charge on an MR tanker at Tarragona is a different data point from the same charge on a bulker at Rotterdam,” he says. Behind that sits a database built from more than 40,000 port calls across over 1,400 ports. HarborLab says its analysts also obtain and verify official tariffs directly with ports rather than relying solely on historical invoices. Comparisons are then made against previously approved disbursement accounts for comparable ports and vessel types, while tariffs carry confidence indicators showing technical managers whether the underlying figure has been independently verified. “Local variation is built into the comparison rather than smoothed over,” Malaxianakis says. For a sector increasingly comfortable using data to scrutinise fuel consumption, vessel performance and voyage economics, his argument is that the same level of attention has yet to reach every invoice arriving from shore. And in husbandry, there is still plenty sitting in the spreadsheet. The company confirmed operations restarted after the remaining protesters were removed from the 70,000-tonne floating production unit, located about 375 km off the Pilbara coast. Two men, aged 48 and 52, were subsequently charged with interfering with offshore petroleum installations or operations, an offence carrying a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. Greenpeace continued its campaign, delivering a 47-metre-long petition bearing nearly half a million signatures to Woodside’s headquarters in Perth. The disruption comes as Woodside moves towards the first LNG shipment from its $12.5bn Scarborough development. In its latest quarterly update, Woodside said the project was 99% complete at the end of September, with gas already introduced into the offshore production unit and export pipeline. articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network USCGC Munro (WMSL 755) transits in formation in the high latitudes of the Arctic Ocean alongside USCGC Storis (WAGB 21) and USCGC Fir (WLB 213) in support of Operation Tundra Merlin, July 21, 2026. U.S. Coast Guard Photo The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Munro has returned to its homeport in Alameda, California, following a 112-day patrol across the Bering Sea and Arctic Ocean that included monitoring Chinese research vessels, conducting joint exercises with Canadian forces and enforcing U.S. fisheries laws. The 418-foot national security cutter covered more than 23,000 nautical miles during the deployment, part of a broader effort to maintain a U.S. presence in the Arctic as Chinese and Russian activity draws increasing attention from Washington. Operating under the Coast Guard Arctic District, Munro monitored three Chinese-flagged research vessels operating in and around U.S. Arctic waters under Operation Frontier Sentinel, an ongoing effort to track foreign activity near Alaska and protect U.S. sovereign rights. The patrol included the July monitoring of the Chinese research ships Xue Long and Xue Long 2 , which transited north through the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone and over the U.S. extended continental shelf in the Bering Sea. Foreign vessels are permitted to transit these waters under international law, but conducting marine scientific research within the U.S. EEZ or on its extended continental shelf requires prior U.S. authorization. The Coast Guard has said its monitoring operations are intended to ensure compliance with those rules and allow a rapid response to potentially unauthorized activity. The Coast Guard did not identify the third Chinese vessel monitored during the deployment in its latest announcement. Munro also conducted joint exercises with the Royal Canadian Navy, focusing on maritime law enforcement cooperation, maneuvering and improving awareness of vessel activity in Arctic waters. The cutter additionally participated in Operation Tundra Merlin, which brought together U.S. and Canadian military assets to test communications, command-and-control systems and coordinated responses to potential threats in northern maritime approaches. “The Arctic is a demanding maritime environment that can test any crew and vessel,” said Capt. Adam J. Disque, Munro ‘s commanding officer. “We also strengthened our enduring partnership with Canadian counterparts, advancing shared domain awareness and coordination across the remote region,” he added. Beyond its security mission, Munro conducted fisheries enforcement patrols in the Bering Sea, where boarding teams inspected commercial fishing vessels for compliance with federal safety regulations and fisheries laws. The Coast Guard described the mission as protecting Alaska’s commercial fishing industry, valued at approximately $6 billion. The deployment comes as the Coast Guard faces growing demands in the Arctic while operating with a limited number of ice-capable vessels. In September, the service confirmed to gCaptain that the medium icebreaker Healy would not complete its planned 2026 high-latitude mission following a significant engineering casualty in July. The breakdown left the Coast Guard relying more heavily on other assets, including the recently commissioned icebreaker Storis , national security cutters and aircraft, to maintain surveillance and patrol operations across the region. China’s growing Arctic presence has become a particular focus. Chinese research ships have conducted increasingly visible operations in northern waters, prompting U.S. and Canadian authorities to expand monitoring of their activities. The Coast Guard has emphasized that the presence of foreign research vessels is not itself a violation of international law, but says continued monitoring is necessary to protect U.S. interests in the region.
